# S2. Coefficient shortcuts and support steps {.unnumbered}

The reference implementation sorts the breakpoints for every active
coordinate. If the derivative root lies in the current Huber segment,
this sorting is unnecessary. With current coefficient $b$, residual $r$,
and fixed $\delta$, we define
$$
 g=-n^{-1}\sum_i x_i\psi_\delta(r_i),\qquad
 L=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^2\mathbf1_{\{|r_i|<\delta\}},\qquad
 b^+=S_{\eta/L}(b-g/L).
$$
For $L>0$, this is an exact coordinate minimizer whenever every residual
$r_i-x_i(b^+-b)$ remains in its current quadratic or linear segment.
Otherwise we use the breakpoint subroutine. The optimized implementation
also reuses residual buffers and score evaluations, and checks all
coordinates at intervals of $c_\kappa$ sweeps. Inactivity is provisional after a
scale change. Termination always requires a full current-scale certificate.

Cheaper sweeps do not remove slow convergence in correlated designs.
We therefore offer a safeguarded support Newton step at intervals of $p_N$
sweeps, for supports of at most $q_N$ coefficients. We define $J$ as the current
nonzero support, including an unpenalized intercept when present, and
$I=\{i:|r_i|<\rho\sigma\}$. On the current smooth segment, the joint Hessian is
$$
 H_J=\frac1{n\sigma}
 \begin{pmatrix}
 X_{I,J}^{\top}X_{I,J}&X_{I,J}^{\top}r_I/\sigma\\
 r_I^{\top}X_{I,J}/\sigma&\|r_I\|_2^2/\sigma^2
 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Using the gradient $g_J$ on this support, we solve
$(H_J+\mu I)d=-g_J$, with $\mu=c_H\max_j(H_J)_{jj}$.
The ridge regularizes the search direction only. Backtracking multiplies the
step by $\omega$ until the original nonsmooth objective satisfies the Armijo
inequality with constant $c_A$ and the proposed scale is positive. After $K_N$
unsuccessful trials, we retain the CD/MM iterate. Fixed-scale fitting uses
only the coefficient block. Each accepted step decreases the same objective.
This addition does not alter the estimator or replace exact scalar updates
by surrogate updates. Disabling polishing recovers the optimized CD/MM
variant. The original unaccelerated solver remains available for audit.



{{< include support-step.qmd >}}

# S3. Boundary solutions and simulation accuracy {.unnumbered}


Very small scales require the closed perspective rather than a numerical
scale floor. At $\sigma=0$, we solve the LAD-lasso linear program
$$
 \min_\beta\{\rho\|y-X\beta\|_1/n+\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1\}.
$$
A dual vector $v$ certifies optimality for the joint problem if
$$
 \|v\|_\infty\le\rho,\qquad
 \|v\|_2^2\le2na,\qquad
 \|X^\top v/n\|_\infty\le\lambda_0,
$$
and its objective $y^\top v/n$ agrees with the primal value.
An unpenalized intercept instead requires $\mathbf1^\top v=0$.
We center the LP dual for the intercept and rescale it to satisfy all dual
inequalities before evaluating the primal--dual gap. A boundary result is
accepted only when the relative gap is at most $\epsilon$.
A small scale triggers this check. It does not itself certify convergence.
This boundary computation also permits continuing the path after a
certified zero-scale solution.


If a positive-scale solve is unsuccessful, the path routine compares its
objective with that of a boundary LAD-lasso candidate and keeps the smaller.
An uncertified candidate remains approximate. At a subsequent penalty, a
certified boundary solution can be continued directly. An uncertified
zero-scale start also permits restarting the positive-scale iterations at
$\sigma^{(0)}$. The full Figure 1 experiment visits every penalty and charges
all candidate selection and boundary work to the path time.

For any feasible dual $v$, we write $D=y^\top v/n$ and we report the normalized
bound $(F-D)/\max\{1,|F|\}$. Throughout 318/360 joint paths this bound is at
most $\epsilon_{\rm gap}$. The largest recorded bound is 0.133. It is an
upper bound on objective error, not a measured error of that size.

{{< include ../analysis/outputs/optimized-paper/rome-completion.qmd >}}

: Returned paths and independent accuracy checks over the full simulation grid. Native completion uses ROME's stopping rule. The Python counts require their stated optimality checks. {#tbl-rome-completion}

The source audit distinguishes compiled C from Numba-compiled Python,
pathwise screening, stopping rules and boundary-LP work. It also records an
isolated discrepancy in the pinned native coordinate routine. For
$x=(1,1,1)$, $u=(-1,0.2,0.5)$, $\delta=0.5$ and $\eta=0.1$, the derivative
at zero is $-1/15$, so zero minimizes the scalar objective. The native
coordinate routine returns approximately 0.08235, increasing the objective
by approximately 0.00501. An installed-R call without screening reproduces
the discrepancy. Adaptive screening avoids it in this minimal example.
This does not establish its frequency in full fits. Native ROME is unchanged
in the experiment. The source checks and reproductions are retained in the
implementation-audit materials.

# S4. R4 normalization and additional timings {.unnumbered}

The R4 mean-shift Path-Alg uses the augmented concomitant least-squares data
$$
 A_{\rm aug}=\sqrt2[X,\{\lambda_{\rm classo}/(2\rho)\}I_n],\qquad
 y_{\rm aug}=\sqrt2y,\qquad \sigma=\sigma_{\rm aug}/2.
$$
The path branch is called directly with zero Gram correction. The unconstrained
DR implementation uses $c_{\rm DR}$ without changing its update equations.
Both methods are compared with CD using the original averaged perspective
objective, not an augmented surrogate objective.

At positive scale, we define $g=-X^\top\psi_\rho(r/\sigma)/n$. The common continuous
coefficient residual is
$$
 \|\beta-S_{\lambda_0}(\beta-g)\|_\infty.
$$
This residual and $R_\sigma$ must be at most $\epsilon_{\rm R4}$, and the
relative objective difference from the high-accuracy reference must be at
most $\epsilon_{\rm obj}$. The comparison therefore assesses solutions
before timing ratios. Setup, prepared solve and total call times are saved
separately. The synthetic trajectory uses seed 91 and a full-rank design.
Coefficient agreement on that example is not a uniqueness claim for every
high-dimensional problem.

{{< include ../analysis/outputs/revision-r4/results.qmd >}}

: Median prepared solve times. Counts give calls passing the common accuracy checks for CD, Path-Alg and DR, each out of six. {#tbl-r4}

An additional four-dataset study uses five paired timing repetitions with the
same optimized Python coefficient routines for fixed and concomitant scale,
common penalties, and identical coefficient tolerances. Medians include only

# S5. Prediction grids and the matched AMP problem {.unnumbered}

For each CV training fold, the penalty grid uses that model's optimized
intercept-only null fit. For the positive-scale concomitant null optimum
$(b_{\rm null},\sigma_{\rm null})$,
$$
 \lambda_{\max}^{\rm con}=n^{-1}\left\|X^\top\psi_\rho
 \left((y-b_{\rm null}\mathbf1)/\sigma_{\rm null}\right)\right\|_\infty.
$$
The fixed-scale anchor uses its optimized null intercept at the fixed scale.
The anchors remain fixed while traversing each path. A shared fixed-scale
anchor would not identify the same relative penalty range for both models.
Each fold fits its own column filter and predictor/response transformations.
Fifty fractions from 1 to $10^{-3}$ define the grids. CV uses pooled validation
MSE and the tie rule in Supplement S1. Final refits repeat preprocessing on
the outer training set. All selected refits satisfy the required accuracy.
Two concomitant inner-CV grids have 49 eligible penalties instead of 50.

![Inner-fold prediction error on model-specific penalty grids and held-out prediction for the first split of each dataset. Filtering and standardization use only the relevant training observations. Certified zero-scale fits are included.](../analysis/outputs/optimized-paper/real-data.pdf){#fig-real width=100%}

The separate matched AMP instance uses split seed 20261006 and the
source-paper global predictor-only filter. This protocol differs from the
training-only filter used to estimate prediction error. All five timed calls
per method use the same filtered matrix and the stated AMP normalization.
Filtering, preprocessing, compilation and calibration search are excluded.
The supplied AMP manuscript is unpublished, and its source is not
redistributed. The source registry records the required checksums.

# S7. adaHuber source audit and matched comparison {.unnumbered}

We pin the archived adaHuber 1.1 source and record its SHA-256 checksum.
For its intended adaptive-lasso threshold equation,
$$
 n^{-1}\sum_i\min\{r_i^2/\tau^2,1\}=c_{n,p},\qquad
 c_{n,p}=\log(np)/n,
$$
our scale equation agrees when $\tau=\rho\sigma$ and
$a=\rho^2c_{n,p}/2$. The complete penalized problem additionally requires
$\eta=\sigma\lambda_0$ in the ordinary Huber coefficient objective.
The native supplied penalty is $\eta_0=\sigma^{(0)}\lambda_0$, determined
before fitting and retained throughout that native call.

The archived adaptive-lasso source computes $r=y-Z\theta$ and then sets
`resSq` to `square(Y)`. Thus the threshold update uses centered responses
rather than the newly computed residuals. We retain the native code unchanged.
The prepared native call reproduces the exported R function, including its
threshold, within $\epsilon_{\rm wrapper}$. We report native scale as
$\tau/\rho$ under the same stated convention.

Our matched adapter uses the package's compiled `lamm` step. With
$Z=[\mathbf1,X]$, $\theta=(b,\beta)$, and residual $r=y-Z\theta$, we first solve
$$
 a-\frac1{2n}\sum_i\min\{r_i^2/\sigma^2,\rho^2\}=0.
$$
We then set $\tau=\rho\sigma$ and
$\Lambda=(0,\sigma\lambda_0,\ldots,\sigma\lambda_0)$. With
$G_\tau(\theta)=n^{-1}\sum_i h_\tau(y_i-Z_i^\top\theta)$, each coefficient step is
$$
 \theta^+=S_{\Lambda/\phi}
 \left(\theta-\nabla G_\tau(\theta)/\phi\right).
$$
The compiled routine increases $\phi$ by $\gamma_{\rm L}$ until
$$
 G_\tau(\theta^+)\le G_\tau(\theta)
 +\nabla G_\tau(\theta)^\top(\theta^+-\theta)
 +\tfrac12\phi\|\theta^+-\theta\|_2^2.
$$
We use at most $B_{\rm L}$ such steps per scale update and require the common
joint accuracy checks before acceptance. This coefficient majorization step
is distinct from our exact scalar Huber coordinate update. The adapter is
new orchestration of adaHuber primitives, not the native adaptive estimator.

The reference solves the same perspective objective at
$\epsilon_{\rm ada,ref}$, and its feasible-dual gap is checked independently.
All returned solutions are assessed by the continuous coefficient residual,
scale residual and relative objective difference used in the R4 comparison.
The fitted scales and direct differences between CD and the adapter are:
